idiom_name: handler struct pairing a context pointer with an invoke function pointer
implementation_notes: C has no endpoint framework, so the structure is written out: a struct pairs the service's context pointer with a function pointer (int (*invoke)(void *ctx, const msg_t *in, msg_t *out)) and a table of such structs binds channels to services; the receive loop decodes the message, calls invoke, then routes the status to the reply channel or to the invalid-message channel. Pointers to functions are C's callback mechanism, so the endpoint object of the pattern becomes one struct plus one callback, and the thread or event loop around it is the consumer. The hand-written form stays the right choice for a custom socket protocol with its own framing; grow the table into a framework only when dispatch by message type is genuinely required.
pitfalls: The void *ctx must outlive the activator, and per-message state must not be stored in it when several threads run the loop; use per-call storage instead.
C has no exceptions: every service returns a status code that must be translated into the error path, and ignoring the return value drops failures silently.
Transport buffers are usually recycled, so anything the service retains has to be copied first.
